1245.bp: When you search the web, you want results that answer your actual question, not just pages that happen to use your exact words. Search engines use a scoring method called BM25 that ranks pages by keyword overlap, but keywords alone miss the intent behind your question. Recently, people have been using AI to guess what good answer documents might look like (hypothetical documents), then searching for pages similar to those guesses. This paper shows how to combine both strategies.
1245.wh: Modern AI-powered search tries to generate what an answer might look like, but it just pastes the AI output onto your original question. Traditional methods for expanding queries—like taking highly ranked results and pulling out their best words to search for again—were discarded because they were designed for keyword-based search, not AI-generated content. The tension is that good query expansion techniques got left behind when everyone switched to AI approaches, even though they might help here.
1245.ww: When you have AI-generated candidate answers, those documents represent genuine possibilities for what the user wants, not random search results. Traditional reweighting algorithms—like Rocchio, which boosts common words in good results—work better on carefully chosen documents than on the raw top-ranked results from a basic keyword search. The algorithms learn which expansion words actually matter by looking at a smarter set of starting points, so they make better predictions.
1245.ap: The researchers take a well-known ranking method called RM3 and feed it AI-generated hypothetical answer documents instead of what BM25 initially retrieved. They let the algorithm pick which words from those AI documents are worth adding to the search, how much to weight each one, and then search again with the expanded query. It's mechanically the same as how these methods worked in 2005, just with different input sources.
1245.po: By reusing old query expansion techniques with new AI-generated documents, they shrink the performance gap between traditional keyword search and expensive neural search methods, without needing the extra cost. On real datasets, they measurably improve how many relevant results appear at the top of the ranking. The code is open so others can reuse the approach.

1246.bp: Recommender systems try to guess what product or movie you'll like based on your past behavior. If you've rated five movies a 5-star and two a 3-star, the system needs to understand that your 5-stars mean strong preference and your 3-stars mean weak interest. Most current systems throw away this fine detail and just mark items as 'you interacted with this' or 'you rated it highly', losing the nuance of how much you actually liked each thing.
1246.wh: When AI-powered recommenders integrate traditional collaborative filtering (the technique of 'users like you also liked these items'), they convert star ratings into binary signals—yes/no, liked/disliked. This collapses a spectrum of preference strength into two buckets. The system can no longer distinguish between 'mildly interested' and 'deeply loved' because the rating structure disappeared into the AI's hidden computations. You lose information your users explicitly provided.
1246.ww: If you can explicitly represent that a 5-star rating is stronger preference than a 3-star rating within the AI system, it can learn that users express preference on a spectrum and act accordingly. By anchoring different rating levels to specific numeric signals the AI understands, the system can preserve fine-grained preference distinctions all the way through its reasoning. Users' nuanced opinions become actual features the system can learn from, not noise.
1246.ap: They assign each preference level (1-star through 5-star) a numeric code and use the AI's internal understanding of those numbers as landmarks to align user-item interaction data. When the AI processes a user's history, it knows which interactions represent weak interest, moderate interest, and strong interest, because each rating level is anchored to a distinct numeric signal. The AI learns to treat them differently during its computations.
1246.po: On real recommendation datasets, this approach measurably ranks candidate pairs correctly more often than methods that ignore rating strength. Users with diverse rating patterns (some strong loves, some weak interests) see better recommendations. The method improves performance without requiring the system to be retrained on different data formats.

1247.bp: When you ask a mapping app 'show me restaurants within 2 miles of my current location,' the system must quickly find all geographic points inside a rectangular or circular region. Spatial databases use a trick called Z-order curves—a way of converting two-dimensional space into a single line you can index efficiently, like a traditional sorted list. But this trick retrieves many irrelevant points far outside your query region, wasting time checking positions you don't care about.
1247.wh: Z-order curves wrap 2D maps into a 1D line to use traditional indexing, but that wrapping creates a problem: a rectangular region on the map becomes fragmented ranges on the line, scattered and overlapping. You must search many ranges to cover the target region, and each range includes many points outside the region itself. It's like asking for 'every person in zip codes 90210, 90220, 90230' because those three codes happen to cover your city—but zip code 90215 overlaps your region and brings in people you don't want.
1247.ww: By breaking the query region into aligned chunks and using a learned data structure (not just a raw curve), you can identify which ranges absolutely contain irrelevant points and skip them entirely. Aligning region boundaries to regular dividing lines means fewer small fragments and less wasted search. A machine-learned index that understands the data's distribution can further prioritize which ranges to check.
1247.ap: They create a learned index called ZPI that understands how data is distributed along the Z-order curve. When you query a rectangular region, they decompose it into aligned sub-rectangles using a careful strategy to avoid creating too many pieces, then use the learned index to retrieve candidate ranges that mostly contain relevant points. They skip over empty or irrelevant ranges by design.
1247.po: In experiments, this method retrieves relevant geographic points 3.6 times faster than traditional Z-order methods, while checking only 1% of invalid points instead of the typical large fraction. For large map datasets used in ride-sharing or delivery apps, this speeds up the core operation that happens millions of times per day. Geographic searches stay fast even at massive scale.

1248.bp: Finding documents that are essentially copies or near-duplicates is a critical problem for search engines, plagiarism detection, and text mining. If you want to know 'which documents are similar to this one,' you need to check similarity against billions of candidates. Traditional approaches use signatures or hashing to prune obviously different documents, but generating and filtering those signatures can be expensive. The challenge is making the comparison truly efficient.
1248.wh: Existing methods rely on symmetric difference—a mathematical formula that asks 'which elements appear in document A but not B, or in B but not A.' This gives a single bound you can use to prune candidates, but the bound is loose: it includes many documents that are actually dissimilar. To filter aggressively, you end up checking many false leads that don't meet your similarity threshold, wasting computation on irrelevant comparisons.
1248.ww: By splitting the symmetric difference into an upper bound and a lower bound, you can separately constrain what similarity must be at minimum and at maximum. A document with many unique words sets a lower bar on how similar it could possibly be; a document with very few total words sets an upper bar. Using both bounds together eliminates many candidates without computing full similarity, dramatically shrinking the search space.
1248.ap: They design a new indexing structure called KIL that maps each document and its length to a numeric key. When filtering, they compute two types of bounds—upper and lower—for each query. During search, they use both bounds to eliminate candidates whose keys fall outside the feasible range. Documents whose lengths are too different from the query are immediately ruled out, then documents with impossible difference bounds are skipped without full comparison.
1248.po: On real document collections, this method is 3-60 times faster than competing approaches. The same idea generalizes to other similarity tasks like finding duplicate strings or similar sets. For companies deduplicating massive text corpora or detecting plagiarism at scale, this cuts compute costs substantially while preserving accuracy.

1249.bp: Modern recommender systems rely on embedding tables—lookup tables where each row represents a learnable weight vector for one specific item or user category. For a system suggesting products to millions of users daily, these tables can be terabytes in size. Larger tables mean better recommendations, but they consume enormous GPU memory and slow down inference. The question is how to make predictions as good as before while fitting the table into available memory.
1249.wh: Every categorical item or user group currently gets the same amount of memory in the embedding table. But in real data, some categories (like 'popular brand') are accessed millions of times during training, while others (like 'rare boutique') might be accessed dozens of times. Giving equal memory to both wastes space on infrequently accessed categories and leaves insufficient room for high-value ones. A uniform approach ignores the fact that your dataset has a highly skewed distribution.
1249.ww: If you use less memory for rarely-accessed categories and more memory for frequently-accessed ones, you can keep the important distinctions sharp while compressing the less-important ones. This is how Huffman coding works in data compression—common symbols get short codes, rare symbols get long codes, and the file shrinks overall. The same principle applies to embedding tables: allocate your limited memory where it provides most value.
1249.ap: They assign each category a variable-length code based on how often it appears in the training data. Frequently accessed categories get shorter codes, rare ones get longer codes. The embedding table is then restructured to store vectors of varying length—short for common categories, long for rare ones. During recommendation, the system looks up the category's code, retrieves its variable-length vector, and proceeds as normal.
1249.po: In experiments, this approach compresses embedding tables to the same size as existing methods while preserving or improving prediction accuracy on real datasets. For large-scale recommender systems, this saves gigabytes of GPU memory and reduces serving latency, directly improving online performance. The approach scales: bigger compression ratios work best on datasets with more skewed category distributions.

1250.bp: Recommender systems learn what users like by analyzing sequences of items they've clicked, purchased, or watched. But real user histories are sparse: most users interact with only a tiny fraction of available items, leaving gaps. Systems often pad these sequences with filler values, but padding with the same item repeated (like 'null, null, null') wastes representational capacity. The system learns the same embedding over and over instead of capturing rich user behavior.
1250.wh: When a user has only interacted with 3 items but the model expects sequences of length 20, previous approaches either augment data by generating synthetic items (expensive) or repeat padding tokens (wasteful). Repeating identical padding reinforces the same embedding and teaches the model that these tokens are important, even though they represent missing data. The model conflates genuine user interests with artificial filler, degrading its ability to distinguish real preferences.
1250.ww: Instead of padding with identical symbols, you can extract multiple sub-preferences from each real item in the user's history and use those diverse sub-preference representations to fill the gaps. A single item the user interacted with (say, a horror movie) might represent multiple sub-interests (suspense, cinematography, actor). Using different facets of each real item as padding preserves the semantic richness of the user's actual behavior while filling missing positions.
1250.ap: They create a module that takes each item from the user's real history and generates multiple different sub-preference representations from it. These sub-preferences capture different aspects the item might reveal about the user. When padding, they cycle through these varied representations instead of repeating a single token. The padded sequence now contains diverse signals derived from genuine user behavior, not artificial repetition.
1250.po: On benchmark datasets, this method improves recommendation ranking, especially for users with sparse histories. The diversity of padding representations helps the model learn richer user preference patterns. It's computationally efficient compared to data augmentation and preserves the actual user signal better than naive padding, making recommendations more accurate for the typically large group of users with limited interaction history.

1251.bp: Conversational search systems that understand follow-up questions face a specific problem: your second or third question might refer back to something mentioned earlier ('What about the alternatives?' after you asked about options). A search engine needs to track conversation history and resolve these references. But most systems are fine-tuned only for conversational questions, losing their ability to answer direct factual searches about single topics. You want a single system that handles both.
1251.wh: Traditional fine-tuning on conversational data teaches the model to handle follow-ups, but catastrophic forgetting—the model forgets its original training—means it gets worse at answering standalone questions. Multi-task training is expensive and complex. There's a tradeoff: specialize deeply for one task and lose performance on the other, or spend massive effort training on multiple tasks simultaneously. You're stuck choosing between narrow expertise and expensive generality.
1251.ww: Two trained models—one excellent at conversational questions, one excellent at standalone searches—both learned from the same underlying data patterns, just emphasized different aspects. If you merge their learned weights geometrically (averaging or interpolating them), you can create a single model that balances both strengths without forgetting either. This works because both models learned overlapping concepts; merging finds a middle ground that retains most of each.
1251.ap: They train two separate models using standard methods: one optimized for conversational retrieval (with history), one for ad-hoc retrieval (single questions). Then they blend the weights of both models using parameter-wise merging strategies. Model Soup treats the weights like multiple recipe ingredients and averages them; Slerp interpolates them smoothly in weight space. The result is a single model that performs well on both tasks.
1251.po: On standard benchmarks, the merged model achieves significantly higher ranking quality (15% improvement) on standalone questions compared to a conversational-only baseline, while maintaining strong conversational performance. The approach requires no new fine-tuning and works with off-the-shelf merging strategies. It's practical for systems that need to handle both explicit questions and multi-turn conversations without training cost.

1252.bp: When you cluster documents—grouping similar texts together—the quality of the grouping depends on how well you measure document similarity. Traditional approaches use word-matching, but documents about the same topic (say, 'cancer treatment') might use different terminology ('oncology', 'chemotherapy', 'tumor'). Recent neural systems learn rich representation spaces where conceptually similar documents sit close together. The question is how to improve these learned representations using structured knowledge.
1252.wh: Pre-trained neural document representations capture general language understanding well, but they don't explicitly use the semantic entities mentioned in each document (people, organizations, medical conditions). A document mentioning 'WHO' and 'pandemic' is about public health, but the representation doesn't know those entities are related. The system treats it the same as a document with similar word patterns but different meaning. You're leaving semantic structure on the table.
1252.ww: Named entities—structured elements like person names, organizations, medical terms—explicitly identify the key topics of a document. If you create a graph where documents are connected by shared entities, you can use mathematical smoothing techniques to refine the neural representations, pushing similar documents closer together. Entities act as semantic bridges that align the learned representations with conceptual structure, sharpening distinctions.
1252.ap: They build a graph where documents connect through shared named entities (if two documents mention the same company or medical condition, they're connected). They apply spectral filtering—a mathematical technique that propagates signals through the graph—to refine the pre-trained embeddings. Documents with strong entity overlap are pulled together, diversifying the representation space. They can also extract high-confidence pairs of documents that should cluster together.
1252.po: On clustering benchmarks, this lightweight refinement improves grouping quality significantly compared to raw pre-trained representations. The method works with any clustering algorithm and doesn't require retraining the neural model. For tasks like organizing biomedical documents or news articles, it provides better topical groupings while remaining computationally efficient.

1253.bp: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems find relevant documents and feed them to an AI to answer questions. The system relies on a retriever—a component that searches for useful documents from a database. Different retrievers have different strengths: some excel at finding factual documents, others handle ambiguous questions better. No single retriever works best for every query type. The question is whether you can automatically pick the best retriever for each specific question.
1253.wh: Most RAG systems use a single fixed retriever throughout, even though evidence shows different retrievers help with different queries. Switching retrievers requires retraining everything or maintaining multiple expensive systems. There's a gap between our intuition (flexible routing should help) and practice (we use one retriever). The challenge is predicting which retriever will best contribute to the final answer quality—that signal depends on the downstream AI's reasoning, not just retrieval metrics.
1253.ww: If you frame retriever selection as a ranking problem—'which retriever produces results most useful to the final answer?'—you can use machine learning to predict the best choice per query. Ranking models excel at comparing items and outputting preference orderings. By training on which retrievers' results led to correct answers on past questions, a ranking model learns query patterns that favor certain retrieval styles.
1253.ap: They define retriever quality using multiple signals, including answer correctness on real datasets. They treat each query as a problem of 'rank these retrievers by expected contribution to the final answer.' They train ranking models (including XGBoost) to predict this ranking given the query. At inference, the ranking model scores each available retriever and the system uses the top-ranked one.
1253.po: Across multiple question-answering datasets, query routing outperforms using any single retriever. The gains are largest when training focuses on answer correctness rather than retrieval-only metrics. Routing generalizes better to out-of-distribution questions than fixed-retriever baselines. For RAG systems handling diverse question types (factual, reasoning, specific vs. open-ended), dynamic retriever selection measurably improves final answer quality.

1254.bp: Sequential recommendation systems use item metadata—a movie's genre, an article's category—alongside user behavior to make better predictions. The hope is that knowing an item's attributes (like 'science fiction') helps the system generalize to users who haven't seen that specific movie yet. But it's unclear whether the system actually uses these attributes or just treats them as noise. Understanding when metadata helps is critical for system design.
1254.wh: Researchers have proposed many ways to integrate item attributes with user interaction history—fusing them in different layers, weighting them differently, combining them at various stages. But without analyzing which fusion strategies actually rely on attributes, you don't know whether the complexity is justified. Different datasets might benefit from attributes in completely different ways. You need a diagnostic to identify when attribute information is truly being leveraged.
1254.ww: If attributes are truly used in making predictions, deliberately breaking the connection between items and their attributes should hurt performance measurably. By randomly shuffling which attributes attach to which items, you destroy the signal without changing the data distribution. Any performance drop reveals that the model relied on attributes; no drop means attributes were redundant. This diagnostic approach works universally across models and datasets.
1254.ap: They create a controlled test: take a trained model, then randomly permute which items have which attributes (keeping everything else the same), and measure how much prediction accuracy drops. Large drops mean the model depends on attributes; small drops mean it doesn't. They run this test systematically across different datasets, attribute types, and model architectures to map out when attribute information actually matters.
1254.po: Their analysis reveals surprising heterogeneity: some models rely heavily on attributes, others barely use them, and the pattern differs by dataset and attribute type. No single fusion strategy consistently makes the model more attribute-dependent. This suggests that attribute effectiveness is contextual rather than universal. The findings guide practitioners to invest in attribute fusion only when analysis confirms the model is actually using the information.

1255.bp: Content moderation at scale—detecting harmful or inappropriate text across billions of social media posts—requires both accuracy and speed. Using multiple AI agents debating the decision improves accuracy and explainability: each agent gives a perspective, and the system reasons through disagreements. But running this debate for every post in real time is expensive. You need a way to get the accuracy benefits of debate without the latency cost.
1255.wh: Running live multi-agent debates for every input means every moderation decision triggers multiple LLM calls, multiplying latency and API costs. Teams have experimented with running these debates offline and caching results, but early mistakes get reinforced and compounded: if the first agent mislabels something, subsequent agents see that error and tend to agree with it, worsening the decision. You trade speed for accuracy, with cache hits amplifying errors.
1255.ww: If you store past agent predictions and reasoning rationales (explanations for why they decided something was inappropriate or not), you can retrieve similar past cases for new inputs without running expensive live debates. By enforcing consistency between stored reasoning and stored predictions, you can prevent error amplification: cases with poor rationale quality are marked as unreliable. New cases retrieved from clean, consistent memory are trustworthy shortcuts.
1255.ap: They create REMICA: a system with a Reflective Memory of cached agent predictions and rationales indexed for retrieval. When a new input arrives, they retrieve similar past cases from memory. They apply Interventional Context Alignment to verify that past cases' stored rationales actually justify their stored predictions; cases with inconsistencies are excluded. The system returns the retrieved decision or triggers live debate for novel cases.
1255.po: On real content moderation datasets, this approach speeds up inference 7-8 times compared to live multi-agent debate while slightly improving accuracy. By avoiding live debates for common patterns and using curated offline memory for repetitive decisions, the system achieves both speed and accuracy. For platforms moderating millions of posts daily, this directly reduces compute costs and response latency without sacrificing decision quality.

1256.bp: Sequential recommendation uses self-attention—a mechanism that learns which past items in a user's history are most relevant to predicting the next choice. SASRec is a popular method that assigns learned weights to each past item, then combines them to form a prediction. These learned weights are assumed to be crucial for performance. But it's unclear whether the model actually needs to learn different weights for different items, or if simpler fixed weights would work just as well.
1256.wh: Attention mechanisms are treated as a fundamental piece of sequential models, but assigning learned weights requires extra computation and introduces more parameters to optimize. It's possible that on many datasets, simpler uniform weighting—treating all past items equally—could work nearly as well while being faster and simpler. But without a systematic diagnostic, you don't know which datasets benefit from learned weights and which don't.
1256.ww: By replacing learned weights with uniform weights while keeping everything else identical, you can directly measure whether the learning is necessary. Comparisons across many datasets reveal that sometimes learned weights are crucial, sometimes they barely matter. This heterogeneity suggests that dataset characteristics—not the architecture itself—determine whether the model needs learned attention weighting.
1256.ap: They train a SASRec variant where, instead of learning different weights for each position in the history, all weights are fixed to be equal. They test this on fourteen benchmark datasets using identical training procedures and architectures. They also decompose the attention mechanism mathematically to measure how much cross-position mixing happens—whether information flows between different items in the history.
1256.po: The results show substantial variation across datasets: sometimes uniform weighting performs equally well, sometimes learned weights are essential. Datasets with low information mixing across positions are robust to uniformization; datasets with high mixing are sensitive. The paper provides a diagnostic tool: practitioners can now measure how much their data requires learned attention weighting versus simpler aggregation. For sparse datasets, the simpler approach saves compute without sacrificing performance.

1257.bp: News recommendation systems suggest stories to millions of users, and recommendation quality directly impacts which stories people see. Most systems use deep neural networks trained on massive datasets, but these are complex and slow. The question is whether a much simpler method—one that doesn't learn anything from training data, just uses hand-coded rules—can match the quality of neural approaches while being vastly faster.
1257.wh: Neural recommenders are slow and expensive to compute at serving time. A system suggesting news to millions of readers simultaneously must process each user's request in milliseconds; complex neural models can't handle the throughput. Simple methods are fast but assumed to perform worse. There's a perceived tradeoff: neural networks give better recommendations but are slow; simple methods are fast but worse. Neither seems satisfactory at scale.
1257.ww: If you use only simple statistics about items (popularity, recency, categories) and users (which categories they read, reading speed), you can make reasonable predictions very quickly without learned models. Neural networks learn these same patterns from data, but they discover them by expensive optimization. A well-designed rule-based system that directly uses these statistics can match learned patterns with zero training cost.
1257.ap: ZoRRO uses zero-weight (no learned parameters) and training-free rules to rank news: it considers user preferences based on past reading, item popularity and recency, category matching, and diversity. Each component uses straightforward calculations without neural networks or training. The system ranks candidates by combining these signals using fixed formulas.
1257.po: In offline benchmarks, ZoRRO matches strong neural baselines. In online A/B testing with real users, it achieves click-through rates nearly equal to state-of-the-art deep learning models while running 600 times faster. For news platforms at scale, this means serving recommendations to millions of users with simple infrastructure. The paper also reveals gaps between offline metrics and online performance, suggesting that simple systems can optimize the right objectives efficiently.

1258.bp: Vector search systems find similar items by computing distances in high-dimensional spaces—useful for similarity search in images, documents, or recommendations. To be fast on huge datasets, these systems use approximate nearest neighbor methods that sacrifice some precision for speed. The question is how to measure whether these approximations are actually working well. Traditional metrics can be misleading because they penalize the algorithm for missing items that aren't truly relevant to the query.
1258.wh: Existing recall metrics—'did you find X% of the nearest neighbors?'—treat all nearest neighbors equally, assuming they're all semantically relevant to the query. But in practice, some nearest neighbors by distance are actually quite different in meaning from the query. A pixel-similar image might be completely unrelated semantically. Penalizing algorithms for missing these false-relevance items distorts your understanding of whether approximate search is actually working.
1258.ww: If you only count retrieval quality based on objects that are actually semantically relevant—not just distance-close—you get a clearer picture of whether the algorithm is finding useful results. This requires manually identifying which results are truly relevant, then measuring whether the algorithm found them. Metrics based on true relevance reveal that approximate search works better on many queries than distance-only metrics suggest.
1258.ap: They introduce two new metrics: Semantic Recall, which only counts items that humans identify as relevant to the query; and Tolerant Recall, a proxy that approximates semantic recall without requiring manual relevance annotation. They apply these to benchmark datasets and show where traditional recall is misleading—particularly on queries with few genuinely relevant results.
1258.po: Using semantic-aware metrics, they show that approximate nearest neighbor algorithms achieve better cost-quality tradeoffs than traditional metrics suggest. Optimizing search algorithms for these new metrics leads to improved performance in practice. For applications like image search or recommendation, this clarifies which approximate methods actually work well and which merely appear to work by misleading metrics.

1259.bp: Pinpointing where a photo was taken anywhere on Earth is surprisingly difficult—visual landscapes vary enormously across the planet. Recent systems use AI to reason about locations, retrieving reference images from databases to help make predictions. But fixed reference databases can't cover every street on Earth, especially rare or changing locations. The question is whether tapping into web-scale search can improve predictions for places not in your training data.
1259.wh: Standard retrieval-augmented systems query a fixed reference database for candidate locations. If a queried image is from a street not in the database—say, a newly constructed neighborhood—the system has no relevant candidates to reason from and makes poor predictions. The database is incomplete by definition. Expanding it is expensive. You're limited by what you've indexed, unable to adapt to new or unusual locations.
1259.ww: If you use web-scale reverse image search—finding visually similar images anywhere on the public web—you can discover similar scenes indexed nowhere in your fixed database. Paired with confidence checks to filter noise, web results provide additional reasoning evidence the system wouldn't otherwise access. You're not replacing your reference database; you're augmenting it with dynamic web knowledge.
1259.ap: GeoSearch combines retrieval-augmented generation with web-scale reverse image search. When predicting a location, it queries both its reference database and the open web for visually similar images. From web results, it extracts GPS coordinates and textual information from surrounding web pages. It applies two-layer filtering: matching visual details and gating on confidence to remove irrelevant content.
1259.po: On standard geolocalization benchmarks, GeoSearch outperforms systems using only fixed databases. By augmenting reasoning with web-retrieved evidence, it handles images from diverse and rarely-indexed locations better than baselines. The two-layer filtering keeps noise manageable. For applications like disaster response or navigation in novel environments, this capability to tap dynamic web evidence provides more robust location predictions than static reference data alone.
